Before we go further, I should tell you what I would walk away from.

The thing founders get wrong is that they think their options are yes and no. They are not. If you say a flat no, here is what actually happens: the other side stops proposing. And their proposals were the only thing telling you what they really want, so you have just switched off your own information. There are three sentences I give every client before a negotiation. The first one is, if you move on that, we can move on this. It refuses and it offers in the same breath, so nothing closes. The second one is, that would work for us if the timing changed. Same idea, softer, and it names the price of your yes. And the third one is the word unless. Unless is the politest hard line in English. We will not sign unless the clause protects the team. Nobody in that room hears a refusal, and yet you have drawn a line that everybody understood perfectly.

Founders accept earnouts too quickly, and I understand exactly why. An earnout raises the headline number, and the headline number is the one they will repeat to their family, to their team, to every journalist who calls. So they say yes to the structure in order to say yes to the number. But look at what an earnout actually is. It is three more years of working for somebody else, on targets that somebody else chose, in a company you no longer control. That is the trade. Sometimes it is a good trade. It is never a free one. And here is the part I insist on with every founder I work with: negotiate the threshold harder than you negotiate the price. If the threshold is set where you cannot reach it, then the price you agreed is theoretical, and you have sold your company for the part that was paid at closing.
